concepts.title: Quantum State
concepts.summary: A quantum system's condition described by a wavefunction encoding all possible states.

claims.text: Between measurements, a quantum system exists in all possible superposed states simultaneously.
Upon measurement, the quantum system is found to occupy a definite state.
After measurement, the quantum fidelity becomes unity for the definite state and zero for other states in the superposition.
The observer assigns weighted probabilities based on overlap before measurement due to ignorance.
Measuring a quantum state forces it to be in one of the measurement outcomes, such as raw or burnt, due to the disruptive nature of measurement.
In quantum mechanics, measurement causes the superposition to collapse into a definite state.
Subsequent measurements on the same system yield the same outcome after the first measurement.

components.markdown: A quantum system's condition is described by a wavefunction that encodes all possible states it can occupy. Between measurements, the system exists in a superposition of all possible states simultaneously. Upon measurement, the system is found to occupy a definite state, and the superposition collapses. After measurement, the fidelity for the measured state becomes unity while all other states in the superposition have zero fidelity. The observer assigns probabilities to outcomes based on the overlap of the state with each possible outcome prior to measurement, reflecting ignorance of the exact state. Measuring the system forces it into one of the measurement outcomes due to the disruptive nature of measurement. Subsequent measurements on the same system yield the same outcome as the first measurement.

It collapses into a definite state corresponding to the measurement outcome
It randomly selects a state unrelated to the superposition
It splits into multiple independent systems
questions.explanation: Upon measurement, the quantum system is found to occupy a definite state, as the superposition collapses due to the measurement process.

options: Because the systems are not actually identical
Due to inherent randomness in quantum measurement, with probabilities determined by the superposition weights
Because measurement devices are faulty
Because the superposition changes between measurements
questions.explanation: When measuring quantum objects in identical superposition states, different outcomes are observed with various probabilities, as the outcome is probabilistic based on the state's composition prior to measurement.

components.markdown: Measurement in quantum mechanics is the process that yields a single definite outcome and causes the superposition to collapse. Before measurement, a system exists in a superposition of multiple states simultaneously, such as a qubit being in a combination of |0⟩ and |1⟩ or a cake being described as both raw and burnt. Upon measurement, the system is found in one definite state, and the superposition is destroyed. After measurement, subsequent measurements on the same system yield the same outcome because the state has collapsed to that definite state.

It collapses into a single definite state

It will always be the same as the first outcome
It will be the opposite of the first outcome
It will be a superposition of both outcomes
questions.explanation: After the first measurement collapses the system into a definite state, subsequent measurements yield the same outcome because the system remains in that collapsed state.

Upon measurement, the system is found in a definite state due to the disruptive nature of measurement, which causes the superposition to collapse. After measurement, subsequent measurements on the same system yield the same outcome, as the state has collapsed and fidelity becomes unity for the measured state.

questions.prompt: What determines the probability of obtaining a specific outcome when measuring a quantum system in superposition?
options: The number of states in the superposition
The squared magnitude of the superposition coefficients
The time elapsed since the system was prepared
The temperature of the environment
questions.explanation: The probability of each measurement outcome is determined by the squared magnitude of the coefficient associated with that state in the superposition, as derived from the Born rule in quantum mechanics.

questions.prompt: What happens to the quantum state after a measurement yields a definite outcome?
options: It returns to the original superposition
It remains in a superposition but with altered coefficients
It collapses to the measured state and remains there for subsequent measurements
It becomes entangled with the measuring device
questions.explanation: After measurement, the quantum state collapses to the definite state corresponding to the outcome, and subsequent measurements on the same system yield the same result, as the state is no longer in superposition.

cards.front: How are probabilities assigned to outcomes in a quantum superposition before measurement?
cards.back: Probabilities are assigned based on the squared magnitude of the overlap (coefficients) of each state in the superposition, reflecting the likelihood of each outcome upon measurement.

passages.text: [...] animated gif showing superposition by using skateboarders. ## Superposition in action Superposition is extremely useful in quantum technologies. For instance, superposition is used to make atoms oscillate in atomic clocks. It’s also important to note that physicists have quite a bit of control over superposition in well-controlled systems like atomic clocks. Physicists can control the atom to be in one electronic state or another. Or they can create a superposition of both states.
